tasks.focus: Start with zero vertical launch velocity; solve time, range and impact.

Complete the four concept checks, review your working and record one improvement. Written marks are self-reviewed; concepts are checked automatically.
tasks.constants: Use g = 9.80 m/s², +x right and +y up. Neglect air resistance unless stated otherwise.

questions.prompt: A ball rolls horizontally at 6.00 m/s from a 7.35 m ledge. Find flight time, range, and impact speed and direction.
A projectile launches horizontally and lands 44.1 m below launch, 54.0 m away. Find launch speed and explain whether doubling this speed changes the fall time.

marking.point: The future root is t = 3.00 s.
Doubling uₓ does not change vertical conditions, so time stays 3.00 s.
Range doubles to 108 m in this no-drag model.

mastery.prompt: A horizontal launch from a greater height, with uₓ fixed, has…
mastery.why: t = √(2H/g), so increasing H increases the fall time.

mastery.prompt: A dropped ball starts with…
mastery.why: Released from rest means initial velocity zero; gravity then changes it.

mastery.prompt: Two balls have equal vertical starting conditions but different uₓ. Their fall times are…
mastery.why: The vertical motion determines the shared fall time.

mastery.prompt: For vₓ = 8 and vᵧ = −9.8 m/s the impact speed is…
mastery.why: The components are perpendicular: √(8² + 9.8²) ≈ 12.7 m/s.

tasks.title: Projectile motion: equal-height launches — standalone task
tasks.focus: Launch and landing share a height; learn symmetry, flight time and range.
tasks.instructions: Attempt both structured questions before revealing the guide. Draw labelled diagrams and explain equation choices. Show substitutions, units and directions. Complete the four concept checks, review your working and record one improvement. Written marks are self-reviewed; concepts are checked automatically.
tasks.constants: Use g = 9.80 m/s², +x right and +y up. Neglect air resistance unless stated otherwise.

questions.prompt: A ball launches at 18.0 m/s at 45.0° and lands at launch height. Find time to apex, total flight time, maximum height and range.

marking.point: Maximum height = uᵧ²/(2g) = 8.27 m above launch.

questions.prompt: A launcher has fixed speed 12.0 m/s. Can it reach a target 16.0 m away at launch height? Justify without guessing angles.

marking.point: Equal-height range is R = u² sin2θ/g.
Its maximum occurs at sin2θ = 1, θ = 45°.
The required 16.0 m exceeds this maximum, so no launch angle reaches the target under the model.

mastery.prompt: For equal launch and landing heights, total flight time is…
mastery.why: The rise and return take equal times; uᵧ/g is time to apex.

mastery.prompt: At equal-height landing, the speed without drag is…
mastery.why: Gravitational potential energy is unchanged between the endpoints.

mastery.prompt: Complementary launch angles share…
options: range at equal heights and fixed speed
mastery.why: The range contains sin2θ; time and height depend on the vertical component.

mastery.prompt: 45° maximises range for…
options: equal heights, fixed speed, constant g and no drag
mastery.why: The maximum follows from sin2θ = 1 under the stated assumptions.

tasks.title: Projectile motion: unequal heights and impact — standalone task
tasks.lessonTitle: Projectile motion: unequal heights and impact
tasks.focus: Land below or above launch; solve the quadratic and identify the physical event.
tasks.instructions: Attempt both structured questions before revealing the guide. Draw labelled diagrams and explain equation choices. Show substitutions, units and directions. Complete the four concept checks, review your working and record one improvement. Written marks are self-reviewed; concepts are checked automatically.
tasks.constants: Use g = 9.80 m/s², +x right and +y up. Neglect air resistance unless stated otherwise.

questions.prompt: A ball launches at 12.0 m/s at 30.0° above horizontal from a 6.00 m platform. Find time to ground, range and impact speed.

marking.point: Select future root t = 1.88 s; discard the negative root.
Impact speed from v² = u² + 2gH is √261.6 = 16.2 m/s.

questions.prompt: A projectile has uₓ = 9.00 m/s and uᵧ = 12.0 m/s. Find both times it reaches 3.00 m above launch and the corresponding x-positions. Explain why height alone does not identify a target hit.

marking.point: Quadratic roots t = 0.283 s and 2.17 s.
The smaller root is rising; the larger root is falling, as vᵧ = 12.0 − 9.80t changes sign.
A target must match both x and y at the same time.

mastery.prompt: Landing 10 m below launch has Δy, with up positive,…
mastery.why: Δy is final minus initial height.

mastery.prompt: Two positive roots for an upward launch reaching a higher height describe…
mastery.why: The same reachable height can be crossed twice.

mastery.prompt: A negative discriminant means…
mastery.why: There is no real time satisfying the height condition.

mastery.prompt: At a lower landing the speed is…
options: greater than launch speed in the no-drag model
mastery.why: Gravitational potential energy becomes kinetic energy.

tasks.lessonTitle: Projectile motion: walls, targets and unknown launches
tasks.focus: Choose the event; work backwards from a target and combine coordinates.
tasks.instructions: Attempt both structured questions before revealing the guide. Draw labelled diagrams and explain equation choices. Show substitutions, units and directions. Complete the four concept checks, review your working and record one improvement. Written marks are self-reviewed; concepts are checked automatically.
tasks.constants: Use g = 9.80 m/s², +x right and +y up. Neglect air resistance unless stated otherwise.

questions.prompt: A ball launches at 18.0 m/s at 35.0°. A wall 15.0 m away is 3.00 m above launch. Determine its clearance above the wall.

marking.point: Clearance = y − 3.00 = 2.43 m, so the ideal point projectile clears it.

questions.prompt: At a fixed launch angle of 45.0°, what speed reaches a target 12.0 m horizontally away and 2.00 m above launch? Explain the positivity condition in your rearrangement.

marking.point: Xtanθ − Y = 12.0 − 2.00 = 10.0 m > 0, so a physical solution exists.

mastery.prompt: To test clearance at a known wall x-position, find time using…
mastery.why: The wall is an intermediate event at a specified x.

mastery.prompt: A rim at 3.05 m and release at 1.80 m requires Δy =…
mastery.why: Target displacement is final minus initial height.

mastery.prompt: A target requires matching…
mastery.why: The object and target must coincide at the same event.

mastery.prompt: A faster target ahead moving in the same direction is…
options: not caught in the ideal constant-uₓ model
mastery.why: The horizontal gap does not close.

tasks.title: Equilibrium: beams, cantilevers and tipping — standalone task
tasks.focus: Draw the forces, choose a pivot, and calculate support forces and turning effects.
tasks.instructions: Attempt both structured questions before revealing the guide. Draw labelled diagrams and explain equation choices. Show substitutions, units and directions. Complete the four concept checks, review your working and record one improvement. Written marks are self-reviewed; concepts are checked automatically.
tasks.constants: Use g = 9.80 m/s². Structures are rigid and stationary; state support assumptions. Anticlockwise torque is positive.

questions.prompt: A uniform 5.00 m beam weighs 160 N and rests on end supports A and B. A 250 N point load acts 4.00 m from A. Find both support reactions.

marking.point: Beam weight acts 2.50 m from A.
Vertical balance: Rₐ + 280 = 410 gives Rₐ = 130 N upward.

questions.prompt: A uniform 6.00 m beam weighing 200 N rests on unbolted supports at x = 0 and x = 4.00 m. A 600 N person walks onto the overhang. Find the position x where tipping begins.

marking.point: At impending tipping the x = 0 support reaction is zero.
Take moments about the support at x = 4.00 m.
x = 4.00 + 200/600 = 4.33 m from the left end.
Further motion would require a downward reaction at the unbolted left support, so two-contact equilibrium fails.

mastery.prompt: Taking moments about A removes Rₐ because…
mastery.why: Its line of action passes through the pivot.

mastery.prompt: A uniform beam weight acts at…
mastery.why: Uniform mass distribution puts its centre of mass halfway along.

mastery.prompt: Two supports share a load equally when…
options: the complete load and geometry are symmetric
mastery.why: Force balance alone gives the total, while symmetry and moment balance give equal sharing.

mastery.prompt: A fixed cantilever support must usually supply…
options: a force and a reaction moment
mastery.why: The clamp balances both net force and net torque.

tasks.title: Equilibrium: ladders, friction and slipping — standalone task
tasks.focus: Resolve contact forces, use moment geometry and test friction limits.
tasks.instructions: Attempt both structured questions before revealing the guide. Draw labelled diagrams and explain equation choices. Show substitutions, units and directions. Complete the four concept checks, review your working and record one improvement. Written marks are self-reviewed; concepts are checked automatically.
tasks.constants: Use g = 9.80 m/s². Uniform rigid ladder; smooth vertical wall and rough horizontal floor unless stated. Anticlockwise torque positive.

questions.prompt: A uniform 6.00 m ladder weighs 180 N and leans at 65.0° to a rough floor against a smooth wall. Find the wall normal, floor normal and minimum floor friction coefficient.

marking.point: The smooth wall exerts only a horizontal normal.
Nwall = 42.0 N; horizontal balance gives the same required floor friction.

questions.prompt: A uniform 6.00 m ladder weighs 180 N and leans at 60.0° against a smooth wall. A 600 N person stands 4.00 m along it. With floor μs = 0.300, can it remain still?

marking.point: Required Nwall and floor friction = 283 N.
Required friction exceeds 234 N, so the assumed static position cannot hold.

mastery.prompt: A smooth wall exerts…
options: a horizontal normal only in this model
mastery.why: The normal is perpendicular to the wall; smooth neglects friction.

mastery.prompt: For vertical weight at distance s along a ladder, the arm is…
mastery.why: The perpendicular distance is the horizontal projection.

mastery.prompt: Static friction equals μsN…
mastery.why: Below the limit it adjusts to the required value.

mastery.prompt: Climbing higher generally makes required floor friction…
mastery.why: The person weight has a larger turning arm about the foot.

tasks.title: Equilibrium: signs, cables and angled supports — standalone task
tasks.lessonTitle: Equilibrium: signs, cables and angled supports
tasks.focus: Balance angled tensions and combine force balance with hinge moments.
tasks.instructions: Attempt both structured questions before revealing the guide. Draw labelled diagrams and explain equation choices. Show substitutions, units and directions. Complete the four concept checks, review your working and record one improvement. Written marks are self-reviewed; concepts are checked automatically.
tasks.constants: Use g = 9.80 m/s². Cables are light and taut; hinges are frictionless; beams are rigid. Angles are measured from horizontal unless stated.

questions.prompt: A 240 N sign hangs from two equal cables, each 45.0° above horizontal. Find each cable tension and show why it is not 120 N.

marking.point: Symmetry and horizontal balance give equal tensions T.
120 N is each cable’s vertical component, not its total tension.

questions.prompt: A uniform horizontal 4.00 m beam weighs 160 N and supports a 240 N sign at its end. An end cable pulls up-left at 60.0°. Find cable tension and both hinge components.

marking.point: The horizontal cable component has zero moment about the hinge but enters horizontal force balance.

mastery.prompt: An angled cable’s vertical component, angle above horizontal, is…
mastery.why: The vertical side is opposite the angle.

mastery.prompt: Unequal cable angles generally give…
mastery.why: Their horizontal components must cancel while vertical components support the weight.

mastery.prompt: For a horizontal beam, the cable horizontal component has torque about its hinge…
options: zero if its line passes through the hinge
mastery.why: The perpendicular lever arm is zero.

mastery.prompt: A cable strength rating should be compared with…
mastery.why: The cable carries the full tensile force.

tasks.title: Relativity: clocks, spacecraft and particle lifetimes — standalone task
tasks.lessonTitle: Relativity: clocks, spacecraft and particle lifetimes
tasks.focus: Identify proper time and proper length; reconcile approaching, receding and particle scenarios.
tasks.instructions: Attempt both structured questions before revealing the guide. Draw labelled diagrams and explain equation choices. Show substitutions, units and directions. Complete the four concept checks, review your working and record one improvement. Written marks are self-reviewed; concepts are checked automatically.
tasks.constants: Use c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s. Frames move inertially at constant relative velocity unless stated. β = |v|/c and γ = 1/√(1 − β²).

questions.prompt: A ship with proper longitudinal length 250 m moves at 0.800c relative to Earth. Two events occur at one onboard clock location 6.00 s apart according to that clock. Find Earth-measured length and interval.

marking.point: 6.00 s is proper time because both events are colocated on the onboard clock.
Only the dimension parallel to the relative motion contracts.

questions.prompt: A particle has proper mean lifetime 2.00 μs and travels at 0.600c in the laboratory. Find its mean laboratory travel distance and the equivalent detector travel distance in its rest frame.

marking.point: 0.600c × proper lifetime 2.00 μs also gives 360 m, reconciling the frames.

mastery.prompt: Proper time is measured between events…
options: at the same position in the clock rest frame
mastery.why: A clock present at both events records their proper interval.

mastery.prompt: At 0.60c, γ is…
Changing v from +0.80c to −0.80c changes γ…
mastery.why: The Lorentz factor depends on v².

mastery.prompt: A proper length 120 m at 0.80c along its length is measured…

tasks.title: Relativity extension: approaching, receding and overtaking — standalone task
tasks.lessonTitle: Relativity extension: approaching, receding and overtaking
tasks.focus: Use signed velocities and distinguish a frame measurement from a closing rate.
tasks.instructions: Attempt both structured questions before revealing the guide. Draw labelled diagrams and explain equation choices. Show substitutions, units and directions. Complete the four concept checks, review your working and record one improvement. Written marks are self-reviewed; concepts are checked automatically.
tasks.constants: Extension beyond the assessed 2026 velocity-transformation equations. Use c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s. One-dimensional inertial frames; +x to the right.

questions.prompt: Extension: A travels at +0.80c and B at −0.30c in Earth frame, with A initially left of B. Find A’s signed velocity measured by B and distinguish it from Earth’s closing rate.

marking.point: The closing rate is a separation rate in Earth coordinates; it is not B’s measured object speed.

questions.prompt: Extension: A ship moves at +0.50c relative to Earth. A probe moves backwards at −0.80c relative to the ship. Find its Earth velocity and interpret its sign.

marking.point: Transform from ship to Earth: u = (u′ + v)/(1 + u′v/c²).
Unlike some backward ship-frame launches, this probe also moves backwards in Earth frame; the sign follows the calculation.

mastery.prompt: The inverse transformation expects u and v to be measured…
mastery.why: u is the object and v the observer velocity in S.

mastery.prompt: Two ships each at 0.60c approach in Earth frame. One measures the other’s speed as…
mastery.why: 1.20/1.36 = 0.882; 1.20c is the Earth-coordinate closing rate.

mastery.prompt: A negative u′ means…
options: motion in the negative chosen direction
mastery.why: Velocity carries direction; speed is its magnitude.
